chapter.title: Lay out the path

cards.body: Why do mountain trails zigzag when a straight line up is shorter? Because only a very fit few can climb straight up, and everyone else stops halfway. A talk works the same way: people keep up when it **swings between how things are and how they could be**, then shows them the way to the top.
cards.simpler: Why do mountain trails zigzag when going straight up is shorter? Because only a few very fit people can climb straight up. Everyone else gives up halfway. A talk works the same way. People keep up when it **swings between how things are and how they could be**, and then shows them the way to the top.

cards.prompt: You're leading 8 friends up a steep hill to catch the sunset. Which path gets the most of them to the top?

options.text: Straight up. It's the shortest line.
The zigzag trail, swinging left and right as it climbs.
The route you ran alone last week, at your speed.

whyNot.a: That's the shortest line, not the walkable one: half the group stops halfway, out of breath.
whyNot.c: That's your path, not theirs: what felt easy to you can lose everyone behind you.

cards.reteach: A path is only good if the group can walk it. Switchbacks add a little distance but make the slope easy enough to manage. A talk's structure does the same job: it makes the climb to your idea doable for a stranger.

cards.title: The hidden zigzag
cards.body:
Nancy Duarte, who has spent her career studying presentations, charted Martin Luther King Jr.'s "I Have a Dream" speech and Steve Jobs's 2007 iPhone launch. Both had the same hidden shape. In her book *Resonate* she names its two levels: *what is*, the world as it stands, and *what could be*, the world if the idea wins.

Great talks **swing between the two, again and again**. Each swing pulls the gap tighter, like a rope stretched between two posts.

You'd think your job is to explain your idea clearly. It's to make people feel the gap first. Then they want the way across.
cards.simpler: Nancy Duarte has studied talks her whole career. She mapped Martin Luther King Jr.'s "I Have a Dream" speech and Steve Jobs's 2007 iPhone launch. Both share one hidden shape. Her book *Resonate* names its two sides: *what is*, the world now, and *what could be*, the world if the idea wins. Great talks **swing between the two, again and again**, tightening the gap like a rope. Make people feel the gap first. Then they want the way across.

cards.title: Killing the Monday meeting
cards.body: Sam has 5 minutes to shrink the 60-minute Monday 10am meeting, so the talk swings: right now 12 people lose an hour each, 12 hours of work a week; it could be everyone back at their desks by 10:15. Right now half the room answers email during it; it could be 15 minutes, standing, each person speaking once. Then the way there: try it next Monday, with a kitchen timer on the table. Afterwards nobody quoted the 12 hours. Everyone quoted 10:15.
cards.simpler: Sam has 5 minutes to shrink the hour-long Monday 10am meeting. So the talk **swings between now and what could be**. Now, 12 people each lose an hour, 12 hours a week. It could be everyone back at their desks by 10:15. Now, half the room answers email. It could be 15 minutes, standing, each person speaking once. Then the first step: try it next Monday with a kitchen timer. Later, nobody repeated the 12 hours. Everyone repeated 10:15.

cards.prompt: Lena has 5 minutes to convince her book club to read one non-fiction book a month. Which plan follows the path?

options.text: Recommend 10 great non-fiction books, one after another.
Now: half of us skip meetings. Could be: a room arguing about a true story. Now: 6 novels in a row. Could be: something new. Then: try one next month.
Start with next month's reading plan, then the reasons, then her favourite author's life story.

whyNot.a: That's a list, not a path: there's no gap between now and could-be, so nothing pulls people forward.
whyNot.c: That's the way there with no climb before it: people get the steps before they feel why they'd want them.

cards.reteach: The path has two levels and a finish. Swing between how things are and how they could be a few times, then show the first step. Without the swings, the steps feel like homework.

cards.title: When you have 10 seconds
cards.body:
The full zigzag takes planning. But sometimes your boss turns to you mid-meeting and asks what you think, and you get about as long as it takes to put down a coffee cup.

Then shrink the path to three trail markers: *What* (how things are), *So what* (why it matters, which is the gap), *Now what* (the first step). Same climb, fewer switchbacks.

One test works for both sizes. Afterwards, **could a listener draw your talk on a napkin**? A line bouncing between low and high, then rising to the top. If all they can draw is a flat line, there was no path.
cards.simpler: The full zigzag takes planning. But sometimes your boss asks what you think mid-meeting, and you have as long as it takes to set down a coffee cup. Then use three steps: What (how things are), So what (why it matters, the gap), Now what (the first step). One test works for both. Afterwards, **could a listener draw your talk on a napkin**? A line bouncing low and high, then rising. A flat line means there was no path.

cards.body: Tom gets 5 minutes to present the team's new app, walks through all 9 features in the order they were built, then asks for questions. The room just blinks. Every point was true, but it was a flat trail with no view. To spot it, read your outline: if every line could start with *and also*, you need a *but it could be*.
cards.simpler: Tom gets 5 minutes to present the team's new app. He walks through all 9 features in the order they were built, then asks for questions. The room just blinks. Every point was true, but it was **a flat trail with no view**. To spot this, read your outline. If every line could start with *and also*, you need a *but it could be*.

cards.prompt: After your talk, a friend draws its shape on a napkin. Which drawing means your structure worked?

options.text: A flat line moving steadily across.
A line bouncing between a low level and a high one, then rising to a finish.
One big spike in the middle, where the best joke landed.

whyNot.a: That's a list of points, not a path: with no gap, nothing pulls the listener along.
whyNot.c: That's one highlight, not a structure: a single peak doesn't show anyone the way up.

cards.reteach: A followable talk has a shape: down to how things are, up to how they could be, several times, then up to the first step. If the drawing bounces and then climbs, the listener felt the gap and saw the way across.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Draw Sam's talk on a napkin and you have the whole chapter. A low dot: 12 lost hours. A high dot: back at desks by 10:15. Low again: half the room on email. High again: 15 minutes, standing.

Then one line climbing off the top, to a kitchen timer on next Monday's table. **Two swings so the gap feels real, then the way across.**
cards.simpler: Picture Sam's talk drawn on a napkin. A low dot: 12 lost hours. A high dot: everyone back at their desks by 10:15. Low again: half the room answering email. High again: 15 minutes, standing. Then a line climbing up to a kitchen timer on next Monday's table. **Swing between low and high so the gap feels real, then show the way across.**

cards.body:
Pick one thing you'd change at home or work. Out loud, under a minute: one sentence on how it is, one on how it could be, once more each, then the first step. Time it on your phone.

Tomorrow: why the best examples come from their life, not yours.
cards.simpler: Pick one thing you'd like to change at home or at work. Say it out loud, in under a minute. Give one sentence on **how it is, then one on how it could be**. Do that pair once more. Then name the first step. Use your phone's timer to check you stay under the minute. Tomorrow: why the best examples come from your listeners' lives, not your own.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now arrange a 5-minute talk so a listener could draw its shape afterwards.

repairedFrom.why: The 'In one breath' card is a purely abstract recap with no image. It also holds the chapter's only open loop, which the 'try' card that follows then buries, so the chapter ends on 'Time it on your phone.' Separately, the What / So what / Now what model is a second framework that no exercise tests.
repairedFrom.fix: Replace the recap with Sam's talk drawn on a napkin (low at 12 lost hours, high at 10:15, low, high, then up to the kitchen timer), and move the 'Tomorrow: why the best examples come from their life, not yours' line to be the very last line of the try card.
